facts_from_discussion: The parties stipulated that petitioner met the 330-day physical presence test of section 911(d)(1) (a 12-month period).
It is undisputed that petitioner earned income from personal services rendered in a foreign country (Afghanistan).
Petitioner timely made the election to exclude foreign earned income.
Petitioner's regular place of business during his contract was Camp Dwyer, Afghanistan.
Petitioner did not leave the base where he lived and worked, except for his trip to the United States for the birth of his child.

Petitioner's family continued to reside in the United States while he worked overseas; they were prohibited from accompanying him, and he admitted he would never have moved them to Afghanistan even if allowed.
In 2014 petitioner owned and registered a vehicle in Colorado, had a Colorado driver's license, was registered to vote in New York, and maintained two bank accounts in the United States.
Petitioner showed no connection with Afghanistan other than the location of his employment: no land, vehicles, or bank account there, and he did not want to bring his family there.
In 2015 petitioner sought jobs outside the United States but not in Afghanistan; he wanted to work in a more livable, less hostile country.
Petitioner paid for internet, received mail, and purchased products on the base.

The court found petitioner's ties to Afghanistan in 2014 were severely limited and transitory, that he had substantially more economic, familial, and personal ties to the United States, and that his abode during 2014 was in the United States.
The record contains a timely written supervisory penalty approval form for the section 6662(a) penalty.

The court found petitioner did not make a reasonable attempt to comply with the Code, offered insufficient evidence that he sought advice, and provided no evidence that he relied on his preparer for advice on section 911.
Petitioner made no reasonable-cause argument and testified that he did little to no research of the rules.
With the extension, petitioner's 2014 return was due October 15, 2015; he filed it January 22, 2016.
Petitioner introduced no evidence of reasonable cause for filing late.
